name: Dual-plane breast augmentation

lead: Dual-plane augmentation is a way of positioning a breast implant. Part of the implant is covered by the pectoralis major muscle, and the lower portion lies in the plane behind the breast gland. Surgeons describe it as a way to combine soft upper-pole coverage with room for the lower breast to fill out, which is how people use it to shape a rounder, more natural-looking breast outline.

It became one of the two most common implant pockets alongside the subglandular position, and it has been the standard approach in implant-based reconstruction for decades. Published work is mostly surgical reviews and case series, with a few randomized comparisons of surgical details.

paras: The procedure is performed by a plastic surgeon under anesthesia through an incision in the breast crease, around the areola, in the armpit (sometimes with an endoscope) or, rarely, at the navel. The surgeon releases the lower attachments of the pectoralis muscle so the implant sits partly beneath it. Surgeons choose the amount of release according to breast type, and recovery plans are set by the operating surgeon.

Reported complications of breast augmentation include capsular contracture (the most common), implant malposition, asymmetry and scarring. Placing implants beneath the muscle is associated with animation deformity, in which the implant shifts when the chest muscle contracts, and with a more painful early recovery than subglandular placement. Regulators such as the FDA have issued warnings about textured implants and BIA-ALCL, and implants are not lifetime devices.

angle.text: The technique changes how a breast implant sits and shows. Muscle coverage over the upper part is intended to soften the upper edge of the implant, while releasing the muscle's lower attachments lets the implant fill the lower breast.

lead: Dual-plane breast augmentation is a way of positioning a breast implant so that its upper part lies beneath the pectoralis major muscle while its lower part lies behind the breast gland. People choose it to increase breast size and fullness, and surgeons describe the aim as a smooth, natural-looking upper slope with a filled lower breast.[1][2][3]

The technique was described by Dallas plastic surgeon John B. Tebbetts in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery in 2001, based on 468 patients operated between 1992 and 1998, as a way to combine the benefits of retromammary and partial retropectoral placement and to suit breast types, such as those with constricted lower poles or glandular ptosis, that do not fit a single pocket well.[2][4] A 2010 review lists the subpectoral dual-plane and subglandular positions as the two most common pockets for augmentation.[5]

Beyond cosmetic augmentation, the dual-plane pocket, also called partial submuscular placement, was for about two decades the most frequently performed approach in implant-based breast reconstruction after mastectomy, until prepectoral placement began to be used in selected patients to avoid muscle-related pain and animation deformity.[6][7]

Evidence consists mainly of surgeons' case series, technique papers, reviews and a small number of randomised trials; documented concerns include capsular contracture, animation deformity, malposition and implant-related regulatory warnings.[5][8][9]

paras: Implants can be placed in front of the pectoralis major (subglandular or subfascial), fully beneath it (submuscular), or partly beneath it in the dual-plane arrangement; in some reconstructions they are placed above the muscle, called prepectoral.[8] In a dual-plane pocket the surgeon releases the muscle's lower attachments so that the upper implant is under muscle and the lower implant is in contact with the breast gland.[8]

Descriptions of the 2001 technique emphasize adjusting how much of the implant is covered according to breast and tissue characteristics, so that the implant relates differently to the lower breast depending on the patient.[2]

In Tebbetts' framework, how much of the implant is covered by muscle is tailored to the patient: in a breast with a tight or short lower pole, releasing the muscle's lower origin and adjusting the gland's relationship with the implant lets the lower pole expand, while the muscle continues to cover the upper part.[2][4] The 2001 paper reported indications, operative techniques, results and complications for 468 patients, all treated as outpatients under general anesthesia, and concluded that adjusting implant and tissue relationships gives adequate soft-tissue coverage with more benefits and fewer tradeoffs than a single pocket location across a range of breast types.[2]

Implants for augmentation are reached through the inframammary fold, the areola's lower edge, the armpit or the navel; the axillary route is described as the preferred incision for Asian women in one review, which discusses an endoscope-assisted high-position dual-plane technique.[5][1]

Implant augmentation itself began in the early 1960s: Wikipedia reports that Thomas Cronin and Frank Gerow developed a silicone gel implant with Dow Corning, the first augmentation was performed in 1962, and saline implants were introduced in France in 1964.[8] For decades the main pocket choices were above the muscle (retromammary or subglandular) and fully beneath it (submuscular).[2][8]

The dual-plane pocket was Tebbetts' proposal for a middle path. His 2001 paper and a 2006 supplement article in the same journal presented it for a wide range of breast types, and the 2001 paper has been cited by hundreds of later publications.[2][4] Surgeons later carried the same partial-muscle-coverage idea into reconstruction: a 2008 paper reported placing tissue expanders in a partial submuscular position, the equivalent of the dual-plane technique, with acellular dermis assisting coverage of the lower pole.[10]

Regional variations followed. A 2023 review describes a freestyle endoscopic-assisted transaxillary approach with a high-position dual-plane pocket, noting that the axillary approach remains the preferred incision for Asian women.[1][1]

Surgeons and patient-information sources present the dual-plane pocket as a compromise: the muscle covers the upper implant to soften its edge and reduce visible rippling, while the lower breast is in contact with the gland so that the shape looks more like a natural breast.[2][8][3] Patients choose augmentation for more fullness and projection, better balance of breast and hip contours and improved self-image, according to the American Society of Plastic Surgeons.[3]

Critics inside surgery argue that muscle manipulation brings its own problems, because the pectoralis can move the implant when it contracts, and prepectoral placement has been promoted as an alternative in reconstruction.[7][11]

Subglandular placement is described as sitting closest to natural breast tissue, but ripples may show in thin tissue and capsular contracture is somewhat more common; fully submuscular placement is rarely used cosmetically because of animation deformity and a longer, more painful recovery; dual-plane is presented as a middle option.[8][12]

In reconstruction, reviews report that some patients with dual-plane implants had pain and animation deformity from muscle manipulation, and prepectoral placement, often with acellular dermal matrix, has been used to avoid these in selected patients, with results reported as similar.[6][13][7][11]

General descriptions of augmentation say that scars typically settle by about six weeks, most patients resume normal activities in about a week, and strenuous exercise is usually avoided for about six weeks; recovery after submuscular placement is generally described as longer and more painful.[12] Incision choices are inframammary fold, areola, armpit or navel, with different tradeoffs for sensation and breastfeeding.[5][12] This article does not give operative instructions.

Subglandular placement is described as sitting closest to natural breast tissue, but in thin tissue, ripples may show and capsular contracture is somewhat more common; fully submuscular placement is rarely used cosmetically because of animation deformity.[8] Dual-plane is presented as a middle option that balances those factors.[8]

In reconstruction, reviews report that some patients with dual-plane implants had pain and animation deformity from muscle manipulation, and prepectoral placement, often with acellular dermal matrix, has been used to avoid these in selected patients with results reported as similar.[6][13]

Capsular contracture, in which scar tissue tightens around an implant, is reported as the most common complication after breast augmentation and a leading reason for revision surgery.[5][14] Antimicrobial technique, matrices and scaffolds, and prepectoral positioning have been studied for prevention.[14]

Other documented issues include implant malposition, asymmetry, distortion with muscle movement, scarring and changes in nipple sensation. A study assessing breast distortion after submuscular augmentation examined how muscle activity alters breast appearance.[15] Regulators have also issued warnings about BIA-ALCL linked to textured implants.[8]

The FDA's patient information describes reoperation, capsular contracture (graded Baker I to IV, with III and IV potentially needing surgery), implant rupture, BIA-ALCL, reports of squamous cell carcinoma and other lymphomas in the capsule, and systemic symptoms sometimes called breast implant illness; it says silent silicone rupture is best detected by MRI and that on October 27, 2021 it ordered restrictions on sale and distribution to ensure patients receive risk information.[9]

Wikipedia's summary reports complications in roughly 6 to 7 percent of augmentation patients and explantation by ten years in about 20 percent of aesthetic patients and 50 percent of reconstruction patients; it also reports that BIA-ALCL is linked mainly to textured implants and that estimated risk ranges from about 1 in 70,000 to 1 in 500,000 women, depending on the source.[12][8] Studies of silicone implants and autoimmune disease are described as contested, with earlier reviews finding no causal link and some later studies reporting higher rates.[8]

Published studies are mostly case series, reviews and technique comparisons. A randomized trial compared harmonic scalpel with monopolar cautery in transaxillary endoscopic dual-plane augmentation.[16] A randomized trial in dual-plane immediate reconstruction compared synthetic and biological mesh within the same patients after five years of follow-up.[17] A Phase 1 registration also covers an endoscope-assisted axillary dual-plane approach.[18] Breast augmentation in general has not been associated with increased breast cancer risk in a review.[5]

The original Tebbetts series reported 468 consecutive dual-plane augmentations between January 1992 and March 1998, with indications, techniques, results and complications described.[2] A 2013 comparative study examined povidone-iodine with antibiotic irrigation to reduce capsular contracture in cosmetic augmentation.[19] A 2010 review states that breast augmentation does not appear to increase breast cancer risk or survival rates.[5]
Wikipedia cites a 2026 retrospective series of 198 dual-plane patients with two revisions for superior implant malposition (1.0 percent) and one delayed mastopexy (0.5 percent).[12]

lore.intro: The dual-plane pocket is discussed mainly in plastic-surgery journals and patient-information pages, where its supporters present it as a balance between natural shape and coverage, while others favour above-muscle placement.[2][8][3][7]

claims.claim: Dual-plane placement gives a more natural upper slope than above-muscle placement in thin patients.
A dual-plane pocket suits constricted or ptotic breasts that other pockets treat poorly.
Muscle coverage lowers capsular contracture compared with above-muscle placement.
Dual-plane causes animation deformity and pain that prepectoral placement avoids.
Textured implants are linked to a rare lymphoma.
